promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Nov 1 2026, 10 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: The knee comes first this week: no tempo, no long run, and a physio or sports doctor visit before any hard running. Running comes back only as short, flat test runs once stairs stop hurting.

flags.title: Sunday's long run cut short
flags.detail: You ran 8.5 of the 13 mi planned and walked the rest. Stopping was the right call, and those miles do not get made up.

flags.title: Stairs and walking
flags.detail: These decide when you can run again. No test run until stairs and normal walking have been pain-free for two days.

flags.title: Flat routes only
flags.detail: Downhills brought the pain on Sunday, so every run this week stays on flat ground close to home.

flags.title: Stop at the first twinge
flags.detail: End any run as soon as the outside of the knee starts to hurt, then walk home. Do not run through it.

flags.title: Next-morning check
flags.detail: A run only counts as clean if the knee feels no worse the next morning. That decides whether the next run happens.

answers.question: Is this an IT band thing? Should I still do Wednesday's tempo?
answers.answer:
**IT band:** I can't tell you that, and your training data can't either. Pain on the outside of the knee that gets worse on downhills, and now on stairs, needs a physio or sports doctor to examine it. Book a visit this week so you train on a real answer instead of a guess.

**Wednesday's tempo:** No. Wednesday is now a rest day, and there is no fast running this week. The tempo comes back after a professional has looked at the knee and you've had several pain-free easy runs.

new.analysis:
## The week against the plan

You ran every planned day, and the first four runs matched the plan exactly. The tempo was right on target: 4 mi averaging 7:59/mi with no fade. Sunday ended 4.5 mi short of the planned 13 mi when the knee turned sharp, so the week came to 32 mi against 36 mi planned.

| Day | Planned | Ran | Knee pain |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tue Aug 11 | 6 mi easy | 6 mi | 0/10 |
| Wed Aug 12 | 8 mi, 4 mi at 8:00/mi | 8 mi, 4 mi at 7:59/mi | 0/10 |
| Thu Aug 13 | 5 mi easy | 5 mi | 2/10 |
| Sat Aug 15 | 4 mi easy | 4 mi | 1/10 |
| Sun Aug 16 | 13 mi long | 8.5 mi run, 0.5 mi walked | 4/10 |

## Why the knee sets this plan

The knee got worse as the week went on, and that is what this plan is built around. It was tight on Thursday's last hill and tight before Saturday's run. On Sunday it turned sharp on the downhills, and now it aches on the stairs.

Pain that keeps growing and shows up in daily life means stop and get it checked. It is not something to test with a tempo. One light week at 10 weeks out costs you very little, but running through a worsening knee could cost several weeks.

## How this week works

Each run is a test, and each one has to earn the next. Nothing runs unless stairs and walking are pain-free, and a run only counts if the next morning is no worse. If the physio gives you different guidance, follow theirs over this plan.

Keep your usual strength work only where it causes no knee pain. Let the physio decide on anything aimed at the knee itself.

## Your fitness will hold

Your aerobic base is in good shape and won't fade over a quiet week. Your easy runs went from 9:53/mi at 139 bpm three weeks ago to 9:50/mi at 138 bpm now. Your tempo pace is well ahead of the 8:35/mi that a 3:45 needs.

## What comes next

What happens next depends on the knee, not the calendar. If this week goes clean and you're cleared, next week builds the easy runs back toward your usual days before the tempo returns. The long run will restart shorter than 12 mi and build up again.

A sub-3:45 is still realistic if you're back to normal training within about two weeks. If it takes longer, we'll look at the target again honestly.
